representativeRepos.readmeText:
agent-browser

 Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell.

 agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. snapshot returns the page as compact text with a ref such as @e1 for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call.

 Install

 npm install -g agent-browser
agent-browser install # download Chrome for Testing (first time only)

- Homebrew: brew install agent-browser , then agent-browser install .

- Linux: agent-browser install --with-deps also installs the browser's system libraries.

- No install: npx agent-browser open example.com .

 Project installs, building from source, upgrade , and doctor are covered in Installation .

 Quick start

 agent-browser open example.com
agent-browser snapshot -i # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-browser click @e1 # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-browser get url # check the result
agent-browser close

 The snapshot for example.com :

 - link "Learn more" [ref=e1]

- Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again.

- CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example agent-browser find role button click --name "Submit" . See Selectors .

- A click fails, instead of reporting success, when the target is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element such as a consent banner. Dismiss the covering element, take a new snapshot, and retry.

 The full walkthrough is in the quick start .

 How it works

 The CLI sends each command to a background daemon that starts on the first command and controls the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Each --session gets its own daemon and browser. By default, the daemon closes a headless browser and exits after one hour without commands, saving state first when session persistence is configured.

 Chrome for Testing is the default browser. You can also attach to a running Chrome with --cdp or --auto-connect ( CDP mode ), select the Lightpanda or Obscura engine with --engine , drive Mobile Safari in the iOS Simulator , or use a cloud browser provider such as Browserbase , Browserless , Browser Use , Kernel , or AgentCore .

 For AI agents

 The CLI ships skills that match its version:

 agent-browser skills get core # the core loop, refs, waiting, and common workflows
agent-browser skills get core --ref commands # one reference, such as the full command list
agent-browser skills get core --full # adds the full command reference and templates
agent-browser skills list # specialized skills: electron, slack, dogfood, and more

 Install the discovery skill into an agent harness from skills.sh :

 npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-browser

 The installed skill is a thin stub that tells the agent to load agent-browser skills get core , so its instructions always match the installed CLI. Or add this to your AGENTS.md :

 Use ` agent-browser ` for browser automation. Before the first use, run
 ` agent-browser skills get core ` and follow it.

 For MCP clients, agent-browser mcp starts an MCP server over stdio. See MCP server .

 Commands

 Run agent-browser --help for the full list, or agent-browser <command> --help for one command.

 Installation

 Flags, environment variables, and agent-browser.json are documented in Configuration .

 Platforms

 Native binaries ship for macOS (ARM64, x64), Linux (ARM64, x64, glibc and musl), and Windows (x64). The npm package picks the right binary for the host.

 Development

 Building from source requires Node.js 24 or later, pnpm 11 or later, and Rust:

 pnpm install
pnpm build:source # builds the dashboard and the native CLI
pnpm link --global
agent-browser install

 Run the Rust checks from cli/ :

 cargo fmt -- --check
cargo clippy
cargo test
cargo test e2e -- --ignored --test-threads=1 # launches real headless Chrome

 AGENTS.md lists the files to update with each change, the docs checks, and the release process.

representativeRepos.readmeText:
NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE)

 Run a managed Kubernetes service on your own NVIDIA GPU infrastructure.
NVIDIA Kubernetes® Engine (NVKE) provides the management plane that platform teams install to create and
operate Kubernetes clusters for their customers. Each workload cluster has its
own Kubernetes control plane, etcd and node pools. You operate the NVKE management
plane; your customers use their clusters through the Kubernetes API and kubectl .

 Preview: NVKE is available as a preview. APIs, configuration and behavior
can change between releases, and we do not recommend NVKE for production
workloads. See Preview status and known limitations .

 Get started · Documentation ·
 Contribute · Get help

 Getting started

 Your goal
 Start here
 What you get

 Evaluate without GPU hardware
 Local quickstart
 A development management plane and a workload cluster on simulated machines. No NVIDIA account is required.

 Install on your infrastructure
 Plan your installation
 The prerequisites and sequence for preparing nodes, bootstrapping a management cluster and installing its services.

 Build or contribute
 Build from source
 The NVKE binaries and the contributor development loop.

 The local quickstart runs on a Linux host or VM, amd64 or arm64 , with at least
 6 CPUs, 12 GiB of free memory and 100 GiB of free disk . It requires Docker,
virtual TPM support and the tools listed in the guide. Follow its setup through
workload-cluster creation and confirm the cluster's nodes report Ready .
On macOS, use the local site guide , which runs
the evaluation inside a Colima virtual machine.

 For a real installation, you supply the machines, networking, node images and
registries, and configure access to NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo) . NICo is
the sole compatible infrastructure provider at preview. The
 platform and version reference lists
validated combinations and pinned dependencies.

 What NVKE does

- Creates independent workload clusters. Request clusters through the NVKE
API or nvkectl ; NVKE provisions machines through NICo and forms Kubernetes
clusters with their own control planes.

- Manages workload cluster lifecycle. Create, scale and delete node pools,
upgrade Kubernetes and replace nodes. See the node pool guide
for the manual steps and preview limits on replacement and upgrades.

- Establishes node identity. Nodes attest through SPIFFE/SPIRE using their
TPM before receiving join credentials. Encryption of etcd data is available
per cluster.

- Connects builds to deployment. Its companion project,
 NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR) ,
builds node images and NVKE components from pinned inputs. NVKE deploys those
artifacts; NVKR owns their build and release evidence.

 The preview needs explicit operator configuration: API authentication is off
and the API uses plain HTTP after installation. Configure
 API authentication and protected access
before admitting callers. The management cluster does not upgrade, scale or
replace itself, and there is no management-plane upgrade or backup/restore
procedure. FDE node images are for evaluation and provide no data-at-rest
confidentiality. Read the known limitations
before choosing an evaluation or installation path.

 Overview

 The diagram shows the NVKE product family, how it sits on NICo and your GPU machines, and which components talk to each other.

 NVKE is not a Kubernetes distribution and not a Cluster API flavour. It is a
 self-hosting factory for Kubernetes clusters : a throwaway seed cluster
stands up a management cluster, and the management plane on
it then provisions and lifecycle-manages many isolated workload clusters
on demand.

 An installation has two kinds of Kubernetes cluster:

- The management cluster runs the NVKE management plane and infrastructure
controllers. nvkectl forms it using a temporary seed cluster; installing the
management-plane services is a separate step.

- Workload clusters run customer applications. The management plane creates
and operates them through NICo, Cluster API and the node agent.

 Read What is NVKE for the operator workflow and
 Architecture for the implementation and data flows.

 Build from source

 Use Go 1.27.3 , the version pinned in go.work , and GNU Make 4 or later . Public Go modules must be
reachable on the first build. Flox is optional and supplies
the repository's development tools; on macOS, it also supplies GNU Make 4.
See Development for toolchain setup.

 git clone https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvke.git
 cd nvke
make build

 This builds the workspace and writes nine binaries to bin/ : agent ,
 updater , controller , nvkectl , capd-reboot-controller ,
 nvke-os-image-check , management-engine , tenant-api and operator-api . Building does not start a
management plane or create a cluster. The node agent runs on Linux.

 The workspace guide explains the modules and outputs.
For local services and test environments, see Local development setup .
Before submitting a change, follow CONTRIBUTING.md and run
 make preflight ; it selects checks for the modules you changed.

 Documentation

 Task
 Guide

 Prepare nodes and bootstrap the management cluster
 Bootstrap the management cluster

 Install NVKE services
 Install the management plane from the deploy path

 Build node images and supply release artifacts
 Get NVKE artifacts from NVKR

 Create and manage customer clusters
 Create a workload cluster , Manage node pools

 Give a customer access
 Access a workload cluster

 Inspect cluster health and telemetry
 Observe NVKE and its clusters

 The documentation index links the remaining guides and references.

 Contributing and support

 Contributions, bug reports and documentation improvements are welcome.
Start with CONTRIBUTING.md ; open an issue before substantial
work so maintainers can agree on the approach.

- Questions: GitHub Discussions .

- Chat: the #nvke channel in the DSX AI Factory Slack.
 Get an invite .

- Bugs and feature requests: GitHub Issues .

- Security vulnerabilities: follow SECURITY.md and report privately.

- Community: Code of Conduct , Governance ,
 Maintainers and Support .

- Releases: release process .

- CI health: the CI dashboard
shows the last thirty runs of every workflow and refreshes hourly.

States and other countries. NVIDIA and the NVIDIA logo are trademarks and/or
registered trademarks of NVIDIA Corporation in the U.S. and other countries.
Other company and product names may be trademarks of the respective companies
with which they are associated.

representativeRepos.readmeText:
MuJoCo stands for Mu lti- Jo int dynamics with Co ntact. It is a
general purpose physics engine that aims to facilitate research and development
in robotics, biomechanics, graphics and animation, machine learning, and other
areas which demand fast and accurate simulation of articulated structures
interacting with their environment.

 This repository is maintained by Google DeepMind .

 MuJoCo has a C API and is intended for researchers and developers. The runtime
simulation module is tuned to maximize performance and operates on low-level
data structures that are preallocated by the built-in XML compiler. The library
includes interactive visualization in native desktop windows and web browsers.
MuJoCo further exposes a large number of utility functions for computing
physics-related quantities.

 We also provide Python bindings and a plug-in for the Unity game engine.

 Documentation

 MuJoCo's documentation can be found at mujoco.readthedocs.io . Upcoming
features due for the next release can be found in the changelog in the
"latest" branch.

 Getting Started

-
 Try MuJoCo in your browser.
Visit mujoco.org to explore MuJoCo on desktop or mobile
with nothing to install, or open live.mujoco.org to
inspect and drag and drop your own models in the WebAssembly version of the
 MuJoCo Studio app (slower than native C, since it runs in WebAssembly).

-
 Run a viewer on your machine.
Follow the Getting Started guide in the documentation to download a prebuilt
release and run the MuJoCo Studio app or the classic simulate viewer (shown
in this video ) on your machine.

-
 Explore our online IPython notebooks.
If you are a Python user, you might want to start with our tutorial notebooks
running on Google Colab:

- The introductory tutorial teaches MuJoCo basics:

- The Model Editing tutorial shows how to create and edit models procedurally:

- The rollout tutorial shows how to use the multithreaded rollout module:

- The LQR tutorial synthesizes a linear-quadratic controller, balancing a
humanoid on one leg:

- The least-squares tutorial explains how to use the Python-based nonlinear
least-squares solver:

- The MJX tutorial provides usage examples of
 MuJoCo XLA , a branch of MuJoCo written in JAX:

- The differentiable physics tutorial trains locomotion policies with
analytical gradients automatically derived from MuJoCo's physics step:

 Installation

 Prebuilt binaries

 Versioned releases are available as precompiled binaries from the GitHub
 releases page , built for Linux (x86-64 and AArch64), Windows (x86-64 only),
and macOS (universal). This is the recommended way to use the software.

 Building from source

 Users who wish to build MuJoCo from source should consult the build from
source section of the documentation. However, note that the commit at
the tip of the main branch may be unstable.

 Python (>= 3.11)

 The native Python bindings, which come pre-packaged with a copy of MuJoCo, can
be installed from PyPI via:

 pip install mujoco

 Note that Pre-built Linux wheels target manylinux2014 , see
 here for compatible distributions. For more
information such as building the bindings from source, see the Python bindings
section of the documentation.

 Versioning

 We aim to release MuJoCo in the first week of each month. Our versioning
standards changed to modified Semantic Versioning in 3.5.0,
see versioning for details.

 Contributing

 We welcome community engagement: questions, requests for help, bug reports and
feature requests. To read more about bug reports, feature requests and more
ambitious contributions, please see our contributors guide
and style guide .

 Asking Questions

 Questions and requests for help are welcome as a GitHub
 "Asking for Help" Discussion
and should focus on a specific problem or question.

 Bug reports and feature requests

 GitHub Issues are reserved
for bug reports, feature requests and other development-related subjects.

 Related software

 MuJoCo is the backbone for numerous environment packages. Below we list several
bindings and converters.

 Bindings

 These packages give users of various languages access to MuJoCo functionality:

 First-party bindings:

DeepMind's related environment stack, includes
 PyMJCF ,
a module for procedural manipulation of MuJoCo models.

- JavaScript bindings and WebAssembly support (inspired stillonearth and zalo 's community projects; mjswan extends these with real-time policy control, interactive force
application, and more).

by Manoj Velmurugan .

 Converters

- OpenSim : MyoConverter converts
OpenSim models to MJCF.

- SDFormat : gz-mujoco is a
two-way SDFormat <-> MJCF conversion tool.

- OBJ : obj2mjcf
a script for converting composite OBJ files into a loadable MJCF model.

- onshape : Onshape to Robot
Converts onshape CAD assemblies to MJCF.

readmeText:
Auto Ontology

 Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own.

 It enables developers to:

- Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs.

- Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems.

- Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer.

- Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API.
Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question.

 Benchmarks

 To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the
 ontology SQL evaluation repository .

 Licensing & contributions. Auto Ontology is distributed under the
 Apache License 2.0 . Third-party open-source components
bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in
 THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . This project
is currently not accepting external contributions.

 Key Features

- Natural-language querying of structured data — questions are translated to
SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM.

- Semantic catalog / ontology layer over relational sources, stored in
Postgres alongside the catalog it describes.

- Authentication & RBAC —using Better Auth .

- Web UI for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings.

- Flexible deployment — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a
local stack.

 Software Components

 Component
 Technology
 Role
 Default port

 Frontend
 Next.js 16 (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4), Better Auth, Prisma
 Web UI, authentication, API gateway
 3000

 Backend
 FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain
 Chat / NL-to-SQL, catalog, datasource APIs
 3001

 Ingestion worker
 FastAPI (Python 3.12+)
 Ingests tabular data and writes embeddings

 Postgres + pgvector
 Relational Database
 App metadata, the catalog and ontology, vector store
 5432

 HashiCorp Vault
 Optional
 Secure storage of connection credentials
 —

 NVIDIA NIM

 Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted
 NVIDIA API catalog ( integrate.api.nvidia.com ) or
self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in .env.example are:

- LLM: nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b

- Embeddings: nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b

- Reranking: nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2

 The endpoints and models are configured via the DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT , DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL ,
 EMBED_ENDPOINT , and EMBED_MODEL environment variables and require a
 DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY .

 Model triplets

 Each model role is configured by a triplet of environment variables —
 <PREFIX>_ENDPOINT (URL), <PREFIX>_API_KEY , and <PREFIX>_MODEL :

 Prefix
 Role

 DEFAULT_MODELS
 Shared default; every field below falls back to it.

 REASONING
 Main chat / NL-to-SQL model.

 NON_REASONING
 Lighter model used for entity extraction.

 EMBED
 Text-embedding model (must match between ingest and query).

 RERANK
 Reranker used by the retrieval flow.

 You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field
left unset falls back to the matching DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD> . So the simplest
setup is to fill in DEFAULT_MODELS_* and override per-triplet fields only where
they differ (e.g. EMBED_MODEL , NON_REASONING_MODEL ). *_API_KEY also falls
back to the legacy NVIDIA_API_KEY for backward compatibility.

 Quickstart

 This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers,
Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2,
 uv , and an NVIDIA API key ( nvapi-... ) from
 build.nvidia.com .

-
 Clone the repository and create .env :

 git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology
cp .env.example .env

 Then set these values in .env :

 DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY = nvapi-...
 AUTH_SECRET = <a long random string, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 32>
 APP_URL = http://localhost:3000
 POSTGRES_PASSWORD = <a new password>
 CONNECTION_STRINGS = postgresql://postgres:<the same password>@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters
 AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD = <a new password>
 PGADMIN_PASSWORD = <a new password>

 Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace
each default password before you start it. .env.example also sets an API
key per model role: replace each nvapi-your-api-key-here with your key, or
delete those lines so they fall back to DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY .

-
 Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in
auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set:

 docker compose up -d --wait postgres
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval
(cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \
 POSTGRES_PASSWORD= ' <the same password> ' \
 uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop)

-
 Build and start the rest of the stack:

 docker compose up -d --build

-
 Open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL and
 AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD from .env . Go to Settings → Semantic
Compilation and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts
immediately and reports Semantic compilation is ready when it finishes.

-
 Ask a question in Chat :

 What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania
in June 2015?

 The agent resolves revenue , product , and state to terms in the
ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the
query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it,
so you can check the result against the source:

 Answer: Revenue for USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in
 June 2015 was $588.80, from 3 invoice lines.

SQL: SELECT SUM(il.extendedprice) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS invoice_lines
 FROM sales.invoicelines il
 JOIN sales.invoices i ON il.invoiceid = i.invoiceid
 JOIN warehouse.stockitems si ON il.stockitemid = si.stockitemid
 JOIN sales.customers c ON i.customerid = c.customerid
 JOIN application.cities ct ON c.deliverycityid = ct.cityid
 JOIN application.stateprovinces sp ON ct.stateprovinceid = sp.stateprovinceid
 WHERE si.stockitemname = 'USB food flash drive - sushi roll'
 AND sp.stateprovincename = 'Pennsylvania'
 AND i.invoicedate >= '2015-06-01' AND i.invoicedate < '2015-07-01'

Steps: Resolved terms: Invoice Line (revenue), Stock Item, State Province, Invoice
 Joined: invoice line -> invoice -> customer -> city -> state province
 Validated the filter values against the data, then executed

-
 Ask something the data can't answer. Wide World Importers has no
advertising data, so a question about ad spend has nothing to resolve
against. An agent connected through MCP checks answerability
first and asks you to clarify:

 You: What was return on ad spend for the sushi roll flash drive in June 2015?
Agent: check_answerable -> coverage 0.5; no term covers "ad spend"
Agent: I can find revenue for that product, but this data has no
 advertising spend, so I can't compute return on ad spend. Do you
 want June 2015 revenue instead, or is ad spend tracked in another
 source I should connect?

 If the UI loads without its left navigation after a restart, the browser is
holding a stale session cookie. Clear site data for localhost:3000 and sign in
again. For other setup failures, see the
 setup skill's troubleshooting guide .

 How it works

 Auto-Ontology works in three stages: it generates an ontology, people certify
it, and the agent answers questions from it.

 The ontology holds three kinds of definition:

- Terms. Business concepts such as Customer or Invoice Line , each with a
description and synonyms, mapped to the columns that hold them.

- SQL attributes. Reviewed SQL expressions under a term, such as a margin or
a rolling total. The agent reuses them, so answers compute each measure the
same way.

- Relationships. How tables join, including bridge tables, inferred from
keys and from the data.

 Generate. The ingestion service builds a first draft from the source
databases:

- Read sources: extract schemas, profile columns, and sample values into the
catalog.

- Name entities: extract terms table by table and map each to columns.

- Resolve relationships: infer joins between tables and bridge tables, and
suggest SQL attributes from query history.

- Write the ontology: store terms, relationships, and SQL attributes in
Postgres, with embeddings in pgvector for retrieval.

 The result is a semantic graph you can explore in the UI. In this example, one
compilation of Wide World Importers produced 31 terms; selecting Order shows
its description, related terms, mapped columns, and SQL attributes:

 Certify. People make the draft trustworthy:

- Test with real questions in Chat, or with check_answerable and
 ask_question over MCP.

- Refine terms, descriptions, and SQL attributes in the UI or through the API.

- Certify names, descriptions, and SQL attributes once they're correct.

 Answer. For each question, the agent:

- Classifies the intent and extracts the entities the question names.

- Retrieves candidate terms, columns, and SQL attributes by embedding search.

- Writes SQL from those candidates.

- Checks the filter values and the query against the database, repairing the
SQL when a check fails.

- Runs the query and returns the answer with its SQL and the steps it took.

 When the candidates can't support a query, the agent reports that the question
can't be answered from this data. Predictive questions go to KumoRFM when it's
configured (see Predictions ).

 In Chat, each answer shows its SQL, and you can view the rows, download them as
CSV, or read them as a chart:

 Auto-Ontology is compatible with Apache Ossie , the
open standard for exchanging semantic models. Ossie includes a
 converter for Auto-Ontology ,
which Auto-Ontology uses to import and export model definitions as Ossie YAML.
Use Settings → Import / Export , or POST /api/model/import and
 POST /api/model/export .

representativeRepos.readmeText:
T3 Code

 T3 Code is an "agent harness control surface". It enables control of the agents on your machine with a best-in-class mobile app ( iOS , Android ), web app and Electron-based desktop app .

 Works with your subscriptions on Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, and fx. If they're set up on your computer, T3 Code can control them.

 "Wait, what are you selling me?"

 Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

 We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the editor that you want.

 Installation

 Warning
 T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity, and fx. Install and authenticate at least one provider before use:

- Codex: install Codex CLI and run codex login

- Claude: install Claude Code and run claude auth login

- Cursor: install Cursor CLI and run agent login

- Grok Build: install Grok Build CLI and run grok login

- OpenCode: install OpenCode and run opencode auth login

- Antigravity: enable it in Settings, then use Install Antigravity and Sign in with Google . No CLI is required.

- fx: install fx and run fx login on the machine running the T3 Code server ( setup guide )

 Command line

 curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

 On Windows, in PowerShell:

 irm https: // t3.codes / install.ps1 | iex

 Then run t3 to start the server and open the local web app. t3 service install keeps it running in the background, t3 update moves to a newer release, and t3 --help has the full reference.

 To try it once without installing, run npx t3@latest . It offers to install the t3 command for you.

 Desktop app

 Install the latest version of the desktop app from GitHub Releases , or from your favorite package registry:

 Windows ( winget )

 winget install T3Tools.T3Code

 Windows ( scoop )

 scoop install extras/t3code

 macOS (Homebrew)

 brew install --cask t3-code

 Debian, Ubuntu ( .deb )

 Download the .deb from GitHub Releases , then:

 sudo apt install ./T3-Code- * .deb

 Arch Linux (AUR)

 Stable:

 yay -S t3code-bin

 Nightly:

 yay -S t3code-nightly-bin

 The AUR packaging is maintained in this repository under packaging/aur .

 Nix (nixpkgs)

 nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code

 The package is maintained in nixpkgs
and includes the desktop app ( t3code-desktop ) and the t3 command.
See Nix installation for NixOS configuration and updates.

 Some notes

 We are very very early in this project. Expect bugs.

 We are (mostly) not accepting contributions yet. Small fixes may be considered. Big features will not be.

 Documentation

 Full docs live in docs/ . There's no docs site yet.

- FAQ

- Connect Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT and other agents over MCP

- Multiple accounts: Codex · Claude

- Run T3 Code as a background service

 Building from source? Start at docs/internals/overview.md .

 If you REALLY want to contribute still.... read this first

 Install vp

 T3 Code uses Vite+ so you'll need to install the global vp command-line tool.

 macOS / Linux

 curl -fsSL https://vite.plus | bash

 Windows

 irm https://vite.plus/ps1 | iex

 Checkout their getting started guide for more information: https://viteplus.dev/guide/

 Install dependencies

 vp i

representativeRepos.readmeText:
Skills For Real Engineers

 My agent skills that I use every day to do real engineering - not vibe coding.

 Developing real applications is hard. Approaches like GSD, BMAD, and Spec-Kit try to help by owning the process. But while doing so, they take away your control and make bugs in the process hard to resolve.

 These skills are designed to be small, easy to adapt, and composable. They work with any model. They're based on decades of engineering experience. Hack around with them. Make them your own. Enjoy.

 If you want to keep up with changes to these skills, and any new ones I create, you can join ~60,000 other devs on my newsletter:

 Sign Up To The Newsletter

 Installation (30-second setup)

 A plugin updates itself. skills.sh copies editable files into your project, and you update them by hand. Pick one per agent, because installing both gives you every skill twice.

 1. Get the skills

 Claude Code
 claude plugin install mattpocock-skills@claude-plugins-official

 Updates itself by default.

 Codex
 codex plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills
codex plugin add mattpocock-skills@mattpocock

 Updates itself at startup.

 GitHub Copilot (CLI and VS Code)
 copilot plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills
copilot plugin install mattpocock-skills@mattpocock

 Then, once, add to ~/.copilot/settings.json :

 {
 "extraKnownMarketplaces" : {
 "mattpocock" : { "source" : { "source" : " github " , "repo" : " mattpocock/skills " }, "autoUpdate" : true }
 }
}

 In VS Code, run Chat: Install Plugin From Source and enter https://github.com/mattpocock/skills . It updates daily.

 Gemini CLI (manual updates)
 gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/engineering
gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/productivity

 Re-run both commands to update.

 Any other agent, or editable files (manual updates)
 npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills -a < agent > # cursor, opencode, devin, windsurf, amp, pi; omit -a to choose

 When the installer asks which skills to take, include setup-matt-pocock-skills . To update, run npx skills@latest update , and re-run add to pick up new skills.

 2. Run /setup-matt-pocock-skills

 In your agent, run it once per repo. It will:

- Ask you which issue tracker you want to use (GitHub, GitLab, local files, or anything else you describe)

- Ask you what labels you apply to tickets when you triage them ( /triage uses labels)

- Ask you where you want to save any docs we create

 3. Bam - you're ready to go.

 Why These Skills Exist

 I built these skills as a way to fix common failure modes I see with Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents.

 #1: The Agent Didn't Do What I Want

 "No-one knows exactly what they want"

 David Thomas & Andrew Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer

 The Problem . The most common failure mode in software development is misalignment. You think the dev knows what you want. Then you see what they've built - and you realize it didn't understand you at all.

 This is just the same in the AI age. There is a communication gap between you and the agent. The fix for this is a grilling session - getting the agent to ask you detailed questions about what you're building.

 The Fix is to use:

- /grill-me - for non-code uses

- /grill-with-docs - same as /grill-me , but adds more goodies (see below)

 These are my most popular skills. They help you align with the agent before you get started, and think deeply about the change you're making. Use them every time you want to make a change.

 #2: The Agent Is Way Too Verbose

 With a ubiquitous language, conversations among developers and expressions of the code are all derived from the same domain model.

 Eric Evans, Domain-Driven-Design

 The Problem : At the start of a project, devs and the people they're building the software for (the domain experts) are usually speaking different languages.

 I felt the same tension with my agents. Agents are usually dropped into a project and asked to figure out the jargon as they go. So they use 20 words where 1 will do.

 The Fix for this is a shared language. It's a document that helps agents decode the jargon used in the project.

Example

 Here's an example glossary (still named CONTEXT.md at that pinned commit, from before the skills renamed the convention), from my course-video-manager repo. Which one is easier to read?

- BEFORE : "There's a problem when a lesson inside a section of a course is made 'real' (i.e. given a spot in the file system)"

- AFTER : "There's a problem with the materialization cascade"

 This concision pays off session after session.

 This is built into /grill-with-docs . It's a grilling session, but that helps you build a shared language with the AI, and document hard-to-explain decisions in ADR's.

 It's hard to explain how powerful this is. It might be the single coolest technique in this repo. Try it, and see.

 Tip
 A shared language has many other benefits than reducing verbosity:

- Variables, functions and files are named consistently , using the shared language

- As a result, the codebase is easier to navigate for the agent

- The agent also spends fewer tokens on thinking , because it has access to a more concise language

 #3: The Code Doesn't Work

 "Always take small, deliberate steps. The rate of feedback is your speed limit. Never take on a task that’s too big."

 David Thomas & Andrew Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer

 The Problem : Let's say that you and the agent are aligned on what to build. What happens when the agent still produces crap?

 It's time to look at your feedback loops. Without feedback on how the code it produces actually runs, the agent will be flying blind.

 The Fix : You need the usual tranche of feedback loops: static types, browser access, and automated tests.

 For automated tests, a red-green-refactor loop is critical. This is where the agent writes a failing test first, then fixes the test. This helps give the agent a consistent level of feedback that results in far better code.

 I've built a /tdd skill you can slot into any project. It encourages red-green-refactor and gives the agent plenty of guidance on what makes good and bad tests.

 For debugging, I've also built a /diagnosing-bugs skill that wraps best debugging practices into a disciplined loop, gated phase by phase.

 #4: We Built A Ball Of Mud

 "Invest in the design of the system every day ."

 Kent Beck, Extreme Programming Explained

 "The best modules are deep. They allow a lot of functionality to be accessed through a simple interface."

 John Ousterhout, A Philosophy Of Software Design

 The Problem : Most apps built with agents are complex and hard to change. Because agents can radically speed up coding, they also accelerate software entropy. Codebases get more complex at an unprecedented rate.

 The Fix for this is a radical new approach to AI-powered development: caring about the design of the code.

 This is built in to every layer of these skills:

- /to-spec quizzes you about which modules you're touching before creating a spec

 And crucially, /improve-codebase-architecture surveys a codebase for deepening opportunities and hands you the candidates. I recommend running it on your codebase once every few days. It is a survey, not a rescue: on a genuinely old codebase it will find real candidates, but it won't untangle the mud for you.

 Summary

 Software engineering fundamentals matter more than ever. These skills are my best effort at condensing these fundamentals into repeatable practices, to help you ship the best apps of your career. Enjoy.

 Reference

 These split on one axis: who can invoke them. User-invoked skills are reachable only when you type them (e.g. /grill-me ); their job is to orchestrate. Model-invoked skills can be invoked by you or reached for automatically by the agent when the task fits; they hold the reusable discipline. A user-invoked skill may invoke model-invoked skills, but never another user-invoked one.

 Engineering

 Skills I use daily for code work.

 User-invoked

- ask-matt : Ask which skill or flow fits your situation. A router over the user-invoked skills in this repo.

- grill-with-docs : Grilling session that also builds your project's domain model, sharpening terminology and updating GLOSSARY.md and ADRs inline.

- triage : Move issues through a state machine of triage roles.

- improve-codebase-architecture : Scan a codebase for deepening opportunities, present them as a visual HTML report, then grill through whichever one you pick.

- setup-matt-pocock-skills : Configure this repo for the engineering skills (issue tracker, triage labels, domain doc layout). Run once per repo before using the other engineering skills.

- to-spec : Turn the current conversation into a spec and publish it to the issue tracker. No interview, just synthesizes what you've already discussed.

- to-tickets : Break any plan, spec, or conversation into a set of tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its blocking edges, written as text in a local file, or as native blocking links on a real tracker.

- implement : Build the work described by a spec or set of tickets, driving /tdd at pre-agreed seams and closing out with /code-review before committing.

- implement-spec : Implement a whole spec on one integration branch. Works the tickets as a task graph, running implementer subagents across the ready frontier for maximum concurrency, then closes out with /code-review .

- wayfinder : Plan a huge chunk of work, more than one agent session can hold, as a shared map of decision tickets on the issue tracker, and resolve them one at a time until the way to the destination is clear.

- retro : Suggest improvements to the coding agent's environment (navigation, automated checks, coding standards, steering files, tooling) after a session, most severe first.

 Model-invoked

- prototype : Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question, either a single shareable HTML file for state/logic questions, or several radically different UI variations toggleable from one route.

- diagnosing-bugs : Disciplined diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions: build a feedback loop that goes red on this bug → minimise → hypothesise → instrument → fix → regression-test.

- research : Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a cited Markdown file in the repo, run as a background agent.

- tdd : Test-driven development with a red-green-refactor loop. Builds features or fixes bugs one vertical slice at a time.

- domain-modeling : Actively build and sharpen a project's domain model: challenge terms against the glossary, stress-test with edge-case scenarios, and update GLOSSARY.md and ADRs inline.

- codebase-design : Shared discipline and vocabulary for designing deep modules: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface.

- code-review : Two-axis review of the diff since a fixed point: Standards (does it follow the repo's coding standards, plus a Fowler smell baseline?) and Spec (does it faithfully implement the originating issue/spec?), run as parallel sub-agents so neither pollutes the other.

- pr : The shape a pull request body should take: a summary as the smallest visual that makes the change clear, before/after evidence that it works, and a merge-danger call (one-way or two-way door, plus blast radius).

- wizard : Generate an interactive bash wizard that walks a human through steps only they can perform: provisioning infrastructure, setting up credentials or CI secrets, walking an unfamiliar third-party dashboard, or running a one-off migration or cutover.

 Productivity

 General workflow tools, not code-specific.

 User-invoked

- grill-me : Get relentlessly interviewed about a plan or design until every branch of the design tree is resolved.

- handoff : Compact the current conversation into a handoff document so...

representativeRepos.readmeText:
Auto Ontology

 Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own.

 It enables developers to:

- Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs.

- Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems.

- Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer.

- Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API.
Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question.

 Benchmarks

 To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the
 ontology SQL evaluation repository .

 Licensing & contributions. Auto Ontology is distributed under the
 Apache License 2.0 . Third-party open-source components
bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in
 THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . This project
is currently not accepting external contributions.

 Key Features

- Natural-language querying of structured data — questions are translated to
SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM.

- Semantic catalog / ontology layer over relational sources, stored in
Postgres alongside the catalog it describes.

- Authentication & RBAC —using Better Auth .

- Web UI for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings.

- Flexible deployment — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a
local stack.

 Software Components

 Component
 Technology
 Role
 Default port

 Frontend
 Next.js 16 (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4), Better Auth, Prisma
 Web UI, authentication, API gateway
 3000

 Backend
 FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain
 Chat / NL-to-SQL, catalog, datasource APIs
 3001

 Ingestion worker
 FastAPI (Python 3.12+)
 Ingests tabular data and writes embeddings
 3002

 Postgres + pgvector
 Relational Database
 App metadata, the catalog and ontology, vector store
 5432

 HashiCorp Vault
 Optional
 Secure storage of connection credentials
 —

 NVIDIA NIM

 Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted
 NVIDIA API catalog ( integrate.api.nvidia.com ) or
self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in .env.example are:

- LLM: nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b

- Embeddings: nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b

- Reranking: nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2

 The endpoints and models are configured via the DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT , DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL ,
 EMBED_ENDPOINT , and EMBED_MODEL environment variables and require a
 DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY .

 Model triplets

 Each model role is configured by a triplet of environment variables —
 <PREFIX>_ENDPOINT (URL), <PREFIX>_API_KEY , and <PREFIX>_MODEL :

 Prefix
 Role

 DEFAULT_MODELS
 Shared default; every field below falls back to it.

 REASONING
 Main chat / NL-to-SQL model.

 NON_REASONING
 Lighter model used for entity extraction.

 EMBED
 Text-embedding model (must match between ingest and query).

 RERANK
 Reranker used by the retrieval flow.

 You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field
left unset falls back to the matching DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD> . So the simplest
setup is to fill in DEFAULT_MODELS_* and override per-triplet fields only where
they differ (e.g. EMBED_MODEL , NON_REASONING_MODEL ). *_API_KEY also falls
back to the legacy NVIDIA_API_KEY for backward compatibility.

 Quickstart

 This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers,
Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2,
 uv , and an NVIDIA API key ( nvapi-... ) from
 build.nvidia.com .

-
 Clone the repository and create .env :

 git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology
cp .env.example .env

 Then set these values in .env :

 DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY = nvapi-...
 AUTH_SECRET = <a long random string, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 32>
 APP_URL = http://localhost:3000
 POSTGRES_PASSWORD = <a new password>
 CONNECTION_STRINGS = postgresql://postgres:<the same password>@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters
 AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD = <a new password>
 PGADMIN_PASSWORD = <a new password>

 Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace
each default password before you start it. .env.example also sets an API
key per model role: replace each nvapi-your-api-key-here with your key, or
delete those lines so they fall back to DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY .

-
 Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in
auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set:

 docker compose up -d --wait postgres
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval
(cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \
 POSTGRES_PASSWORD= ' <the same password> ' \
 uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop)

-
 Build and start the rest of the stack:

 docker compose up -d --build

-
 Open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL and
 AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD from .env . Go to Settings → Semantic
Compilation and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts
immediately and reports Semantic compilation is ready when it finishes.

-
 Ask a question in Chat :

 What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania
in June 2015?

 The agent resolves revenue , product , and state to terms in the
ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the
query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it,
so you can check the result against the source:

 Answer: Revenue for USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in
 June 2015 was $588.80, from 3 invoice lines.

SQL: SELECT SUM(il.extendedprice) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS invoice_lines
 FROM sales.invoicelines il
 JOIN sales.invoices i ON il.invoiceid = i.invoiceid
 JOIN warehouse.stockitems si ON il.stockitemid = si.stockitemid
 JOIN sales.customers c ON i.customerid = c.customerid
 JOIN application.cities ct ON c.deliverycityid = ct.cityid
 JOIN application.stateprovinces sp ON ct.stateprovinceid = sp.stateprovinceid
 WHERE si.stockitemname = 'USB food flash drive - sushi roll'
 AND sp.stateprovincename = 'Pennsylvania'
 AND i.invoicedate >= '2015-06-01' AND i.invoicedate < '2015-07-01'

Steps: Resolved terms: Invoice Line (revenue), Stock Item, State Province, Invoice
 Joined: invoice line -> invoice -> customer -> city -> state province
 Validated the filter values against the data, then executed

-
 Ask something the data can't answer. Wide World Importers has no
advertising data, so a question about ad spend has nothing to resolve
against. An agent connected through MCP checks answerability
first and asks you to clarify:

 You: What was return on ad spend for the sushi roll flash drive in June 2015?
Agent: check_answerable -> coverage 0.5; no term covers "ad spend"
Agent: I can find revenue for that product, but this data has no
 advertising spend, so I can't compute return on ad spend. Do you
 want June 2015 revenue instead, or is ad spend tracked in another
 source I should connect?

 If the UI loads without its left navigation after a restart, the browser is
holding a stale session cookie. Clear site data for localhost:3000 and sign in
again. For other setup failures, see the
 setup skill's troubleshooting guide .

 How it works

 Auto-Ontology works in three stages: it generates an ontology, people certify
it, and the agent answers questions from it.

 The ontology holds three kinds of definition:

- Terms. Business concepts such as Customer or Invoice Line , each with a
description and synonyms, mapped to the columns that hold them.

- SQL attributes. Reviewed SQL expressions under a term, such as a margin or
a rolling total. The agent reuses them, so answers compute each measure the
same way.

- Relationships. How tables join, including bridge tables, inferred from
keys and from the data.

 Generate. The ingestion service builds a first draft from the source
databases:

- Read sources: extract schemas, profile columns, and sample values into the
catalog.

- Name entities: extract terms table by table and map each to columns.

- Resolve relationships: infer joins between tables and bridge tables, and
suggest SQL attributes from query history.

- Write the ontology: store terms, relationships, and SQL attributes in
Postgres, with embeddings in pgvector for retrieval.

 The result is a semantic graph you can explore in the UI. In this example, one
compilation of Wide World Importers produced 31 terms; selecting Order shows
its description, related terms, mapped columns, and SQL attributes:

 Certify. People make the draft trustworthy:

- Test with real questions in Chat, or with check_answerable and
 ask_question over MCP.

- Refine terms, descriptions, and SQL attributes in the UI or through the API.

- Certify names, descriptions, and SQL attributes once they're correct.

 Answer. For each question, the agent:

- Classifies the intent and extracts the entities the question names.

- Retrieves candidate terms, columns, and SQL attributes by embedding search.

- Writes SQL from those candidates.

- Checks the filter values and the query against the database, repairing the
SQL when a check fails.

- Runs the query and returns the answer with its SQL and the steps it took.

 When the candidates can't support a query, the agent reports that the question
can't be answered from this data. Predictive questions go to KumoRFM when it's
configured (see Predictions ).

 In Chat, each answer shows its SQL, and you can view the rows, download them as
CSV, or read them as a chart:

 Auto-Ontology is compatible with Apache Ossie , the
open standard for exchanging semantic models. Ossie includes a
 converter for Auto-Ontology ,
which Auto-Ontology uses to import and export model definitions as Ossie YAML.
Use Settings → Import / Export , or POST /api/model/import and
 POST /api/model/export .

 Your coding agent forgets everything between sessions. Claude-Mem remembers for it.

 Quick Start •
 How It Works •
 Search Tools •
 Documentation •
 Configuration •
 Troubleshooting •
 License

 Every new session, your agent starts from zero. It re-reads the same files, re-asks the same questions, and walks back into mistakes you already fixed together.

 Claude-Mem runs a second agent beside it that takes notes while it works. The next session starts with a short index of what matters, and pulls in the details only when it needs them. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and 11 more agents. Copilot CLI, Goose, Roo Code and Warp can search your memory, but their sessions aren't recorded.

 Quick Start

 Installing for someone as an AI agent? Run npx claude-mem install --runtime worker on their computer in an interactive terminal (enable PTY in your shell tool). It first asks in the terminal which agents to set up and, for Claude Code, whether to disable native auto-memory (and whether to overwrite an existing install). Relay each question to the user and type their answer, or pass --ide <id> to skip the first one. Keep the installer running. When it prints Continue setup in your browser , open that URL in the user's browser if the installer hasn't already opened it. Let the user go through setup and make their own choices, including the usage-analytics question the installer may ask at the end. If you can't run an interactive terminal on their computer, give them the command to run locally.

 npx claude-mem install

 The installer finds the agents on your machine and asks which ones to set up. Then just start working: observations stream in from your first prompt, and your second session in a project opens with memory from the first. (Copilot CLI, Goose, Roo Code and Warp get memory search only, so their sessions don't add to it.)

 The installer sets everything up first, then asks you to sign in to claude-mem in your browser (email magic link, no card required to sign in). Choosing the claude-mem observer then starts its 30 Day Free Trial on a checkout page that asks for a payment method; once it completes, the installer saves your memory key. With the observer, memory runs off-plan, so you get up to 100% more usage from your plan. When the free trial ends, memory automatically falls back to your Anthropic plan unless you subscribe. After sign-in you pick your memory provider: the claude-mem observer, your own OpenRouter or Gemini key, or your Anthropic plan.

 Prefer to skip the sign-in? Pass an explicit --provider flag, set CLAUDE_MEM_ONLINE_OPTIN=false , or run in CI/non-interactive shells — the installer completes without any account interaction.

 Your memory lives in ~/.claude-mem on your machine. Cloud sync is opt-in. Anonymous usage analytics are on by default; npx claude-mem telemetry disable turns them off ( what's collected ).

 Or install from the plugin marketplace inside Claude Code:

 /plugin marketplace add thedotmack/claude-mem

/plugin install claude-mem

 Restart Claude Code. Context from previous sessions will automatically appear in new sessions.

 Note: Claude-Mem is also published on npm, but npm install -g claude-mem installs the SDK/library only — it does not register the plugin hooks or set up the worker service. Always install via npx claude-mem install or the /plugin commands above.

 Other agents

 npx claude-mem install covers every supported agent. To set up one agent directly, pass --ide .

 OpenCode (1.3.4 or later, including OpenCode 2). Restart OpenCode after installing.

 npx claude-mem install --ide opencode

 T3 Code (Codex and Claude Code providers). The installer discovers T3 Code's enabled providers, registers native Claude-Mem plugins in their configured homes, and supports T3-managed Codex. Restart T3 Code, trust the provider's hooks when prompted, and start a new thread. See the T3 Code integration guide for custom server settings, status, and removal.

 npx claude-mem install --ide t3code

 Antigravity CLI ( setup guide ):

 npx claude-mem install --ide antigravity

 OMP (Oh My Pi):

 npx claude-mem install --ide omp

 Pi and DeepSeek Harness use the worker runtime. See native harness setup for capture, recall, and troubleshooting.

 npx claude-mem install --ide pi
npx claude-mem install --ide dsh --dsh-profile tui

 Grok Bot: see Grok Bot below.

 npx claude-mem install --ide grok-bot

 The full list of --ide values is in npx claude-mem --help .

 Grok Bot

 Grok Bot has no host hooks, so we watch the chat log files. Default is CMEM Pro, the hosted memory. Local observer is opt-in: --provider host . Installing this plugin does not install Cursor.

 Opt-in awareness push: needle observations ( decision , bugfix , security_alert , sensitive ) are appended as dated - YYYY-MM-DD [awareness] … lines into that bot's memory/log/YYYY-MM.md . Grok Bot already re-reads the log from disk. This does not write profile.md , user-memory, or project memory. Enable with CLAUDE_MEM_GROK_BOT_AWARENESS_ENABLED=true and set CLAUDE_MEM_GROK_BOT_AWARENESS_AGENT_IDS to your agent UUIDs (empty by default).

 🦞 OpenClaw Gateway

 Install claude-mem as a persistent memory plugin on OpenClaw gateways with a single command:

 curl -fsSL https://install.cmem.ai/openclaw.sh | bash

 The installer handles dependencies, plugin setup, AI provider configuration, worker startup, and optional real-time observation feeds to Telegram, Discord, Slack, and more. See the OpenClaw Integration Guide for details.

 What You Get

- 🧠 The next session starts where the last one left off. Each session opens with a compact index of past observations, layered so the agent opens full details only when it needs them, and the header can show what each layer costs in tokens.

- 🔍 Find anything you worked on. The mem-search skill searches your project history in three steps (index, timeline, details), so the agent spends tokens only on what it opens.

- 🖥️ Watch it work, and keep track of yours. My Work shows live requests, progress, human handoffs and a saved review queue at the worker URL printed on startup. Guide . Memory, sessions and settings remain at /viewer .

- 👥 Share with your team, if you want. TeamBrain is an optional shared workspace beside My Work, with real team work lists, member attribution and linked findings. Each person chooses what to share; personal requests and review notes stay separate. Set up a team .

- 💻 Search from Claude Desktop. Search your memory from Claude Desktop conversations.

- 🔒 Keep secrets out. Wrap anything in <private> tags and it never gets stored.

- 🖼️ Screenshots, kept by default. Keep converted copies of tool screenshots under ~/.claude-mem/media-v1/ and show them in My Work, upload them to cmem.ai only when Cloud Sync is on, and send them to the observer model only when image inference is separately enabled. Turn it off with the "Keep images" switch in Settings ( details ).

- ⚙️ Choose what gets injected. Fine-grained settings for what context a new session starts with.

- 🤖 Nothing to remember to do. It runs on its own once installed.

- 🔗 Point back to past work. Every observation has an ID you can cite through the worker API or open in the web viewer.

 Documentation

 📚 View Full Documentation - Browse on official website

 Getting Started

- Installation Guide - Quick start & advanced installation

- Usage Guide - How Claude-Mem works automatically

- Search Tools - Query your project history with natural language

- Cloud Sync - Back up your memory to cmem.ai — no daemon, the worker syncs on write

 Best Practices

- Context Engineering - AI agent context optimization principles

- Progressive Disclosure - Philosophy behind Claude-Mem's context priming strategy

 Architecture

- Overview - System components & data flow

- Architecture Evolution - The journey from v3 to v5

- Hooks Architecture - How Claude-Mem uses lifecycle hooks

- Hooks Reference - Every hook entry explained

- Worker Service - HTTP API & Bun management

- Database - SQLite schema & FTS5 search

- Search Architecture - Hybrid search with Chroma vector database

 Configuration & Development

- Configuration - Environment variables & settings

- Development - Building, testing, contributing

- Troubleshooting - Common issues & solutions

 How It Works

- Your agent works. Hooks in your agent hand each tool call (what it reads, edits and runs) to a small local worker.

- The observer takes notes. A second agent turns that activity into short observations, and writes a summary when the session ends.

- The next session starts with them. When a session starts, your agent gets a compact index of the observations that matter for this project, and fetches full details only when it needs them.

 Memory injection starts on your second session in a project. To front-load a whole repo instead, run /learn-codebase (~5 minutes on a typical repo, optional).

 See Architecture Overview for details.

 How it fits together

 For contributors, the main parts and where they live:

- The claude-mem command ( src/npx-cli/index.ts ): install, repair, doctor, start, search and the rest. The installer puts a small launcher on PATH so hooks can run claude-mem directly.

- Hooks ( src/cli/hook-command.ts , one adapter per agent in src/cli/adapters/ ): each agent event runs one shell-free command, such as claude-mem hook claude-code <event> . For Claude Code that's Setup ( claude --init / --maintenance ), SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, SubagentStop and SessionEnd.

- The worker ( src/services/worker-service.ts , routes in src/services/worker/http/routes/ ): a local HTTP service managed by Bun. It takes tool activity from the hooks, runs the observer, and serves the viewer and search.

- The observer (prompts in src/sdk/ , one provider per model source in src/services/worker/ , such as ClaudeProvider.ts and OpenRouterProvider.ts ): turns tool activity into observations and summaries.

- Storage ( src/services/sqlite/ ): SQLite at ~/.claude-mem/claude-mem.db holds sessions, observations and summaries. Chroma adds semantic search on top of SQLite's keyword search ( src/services/worker/search/ ).

- Context ( src/services/context/ ): builds the block a new session starts with.

- Search ( src/servers/mcp-server.ts , plugin/skills/mem-search/ ): the MCP tools and the mem-search skill that drives them.

- The viewer ( src/ui/viewer/ at /viewer , src/ui/my-work/ at / ): memory, sessions and settings, plus My Work.

- The built plugin ( plugin/ ): written by npm run build ; edit src/ , not the generated scripts.

 The words we use for each of these, and the story they tell, are in docs/story.md .

 MCP Search Tools

 Search runs through three MCP tools in a token-efficient three-step workflow. The mem-search skill drives it for you:

 The three steps:

- search - Get compact index with IDs (~50-100 tokens/result)

- timeline - Get chronological context around interesting results

- get_observations - Fetch full details ONLY for filtered IDs (~500-1,000 tokens/result)

 Step by step:

- Your agent uses MCP tools to search your memory

- Start with search to get an index of results

- Use timeline to see what was happening around specific observations

- Use get_observations to fetch full details for relevant IDs

- ~10x token savings by filtering before fetching details

representativeRepos.readmeText:
T3 Code

 T3 Code is an "agent harness control surface". It enables control of the agents on your machine with a best-in-class mobile app ( iOS , Android ), web app and Electron-based desktop app .

 Works with your subscriptions on Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, and fx. If they're set up on your computer, T3 Code can control them.

 "Wait, what are you selling me?"

 Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

 We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the editor that you want.

 Installation

 Warning
 T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity, and fx. Install and authenticate at least one provider before use:

- Codex: install Codex CLI and run codex login

- Claude: install Claude Code and run claude auth login

- Cursor: install Cursor CLI and run agent login

- Grok Build: install Grok Build CLI and run grok login

- OpenCode: install OpenCode and run opencode auth login

- Antigravity: enable it in Settings, then use Install Antigravity and Sign in with Google . No CLI is required.

- fx: install fx and run fx login on the machine running the T3 Code server ( setup guide )

 Command line

 curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

 On Windows, in PowerShell:

 irm https: // t3.codes / install.ps1 | iex

 Then run t3 to start the server and open the local web app. t3 service install keeps it running in the background, t3 update moves to a newer release, and t3 --help has the full reference.

 To try it once without installing, run npx t3@latest . It offers to install the t3 command for you.

 Desktop app

 Install the latest version of the desktop app from GitHub Releases , or from your favorite package registry:

 Windows ( winget )

 winget install T3Tools.T3Code

 Windows ( scoop )

 scoop install extras/t3code

 macOS (Homebrew)

 brew install --cask t3-code

 Debian, Ubuntu ( .deb )

 Download the .deb from GitHub Releases , then:

 sudo apt install ./T3-Code- * .deb

 Arch Linux (AUR)

 Stable:

 yay -S t3code-bin

 Nightly:

 yay -S t3code-nightly-bin

 The AUR packaging is maintained in this repository under packaging/aur .

 Nix (nixpkgs)

 nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code

 The package is maintained in nixpkgs
and includes the desktop app ( t3code-desktop ) and the t3 command.
See Nix installation for NixOS configuration and updates.

 Some notes

 We are very very early in this project. Expect bugs.

 We are (mostly) not accepting contributions yet. Small fixes may be considered. Big features will not be.

 Documentation

 Full docs live in docs/ . There's no docs site yet.

- FAQ

- Install and first run

- Permission modes

- Keyboard shortcuts

- Project settings

- Appearance preferences

- Remote access from a phone or another machine

- Connect Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT and other agents over MCP

- Keeping app and server in sync

- Source control integrations

- Multiple accounts: Codex · Claude

- Run T3 Code as a background service

 Building from source? Start at docs/internals/overview.md .

 If you REALLY want to contribute still.... read this first

 Install vp

 T3 Code uses Vite+ so you'll need to install the global vp command-line tool.

 macOS / Linux

 curl -fsSL https://vite.plus | bash

 Windows

 irm https://vite.plus/ps1 | iex

 Checkout their getting started guide for more information: https://viteplus.dev/guide/

 Install dependencies

 vp i

 Read CONTRIBUTING.md before reporting a bug or opening a PR.

 Have a feature request? Start an Ideas discussion .

 Need support? Join the Discord .

representativeRepos.readmeText:
Skills For Real Engineers

 My agent skills that I use every day to do real engineering - not vibe coding.

 Developing real applications is hard. Approaches like GSD, BMAD, and Spec-Kit try to help by owning the process. But while doing so, they take away your control and make bugs in the process hard to resolve.

 These skills are designed to be small, easy to adapt, and composable. They work with any model. They're based on decades of engineering experience. Hack around with them. Make them your own. Enjoy.

 If you want to keep up with changes to these skills, and any new ones I create, you can join ~60,000 other devs on my newsletter:

 Sign Up To The Newsletter

 Installation (30-second setup)

 A plugin updates itself. skills.sh copies editable files into your project, and you update them by hand. Pick one per agent, because installing both gives you every skill twice.

 1. Get the skills

 Claude Code
 claude plugin install mattpocock-skills@claude-plugins-official

 Updates itself by default.

 Codex
 codex plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills
codex plugin add mattpocock-skills@mattpocock

 Updates itself at startup.

 GitHub Copilot (CLI and VS Code)
 copilot plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills
copilot plugin install mattpocock-skills@mattpocock

 Then, once, add to ~/.copilot/settings.json :

 {
 "extraKnownMarketplaces" : {
 "mattpocock" : { "source" : { "source" : " github " , "repo" : " mattpocock/skills " }, "autoUpdate" : true }
 }
}

 In VS Code, run Chat: Install Plugin From Source and enter https://github.com/mattpocock/skills . It updates daily.

 Gemini CLI (manual updates)
 gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/engineering
gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/productivity

 Re-run both commands to update.

 Any other agent, or editable files (manual updates)
 npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills -a < agent > # cursor, opencode, devin, windsurf, amp, pi; omit -a to choose

 When the installer asks which skills to take, include setup-matt-pocock-skills . To update, run npx skills@latest update , and re-run add to pick up new skills.

 2. Run /setup-matt-pocock-skills

 In your agent, run it once per repo. It will:

- Ask you which issue tracker you want to use (GitHub, GitLab, local files, or anything else you describe)

- Ask you what labels you apply to tickets when you triage them ( /triage uses labels)

- Ask you where you want to save any docs we create

 3. Bam - you're ready to go.

 Why These Skills Exist

 I built these skills as a way to fix common failure modes I see with Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents.

 #1: The Agent Didn't Do What I Want

 "No-one knows exactly what they want"

 David Thomas & Andrew Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer

 The Problem . The most common failure mode in software development is misalignment. You think the dev knows what you want. Then you see what they've built - and you realize it didn't understand you at all.

 This is just the same in the AI age. There is a communication gap between you and the agent. The fix for this is a grilling session - getting the agent to ask you detailed questions about what you're building.

 The Fix is to use:

- /grill-me - for non-code uses

- /grill-with-docs - same as /grill-me , but adds more goodies (see below)

 These are my most popular skills. They help you align with the agent before you get started, and think deeply about the change you're making. Use them every time you want to make a change.

 #2: The Agent Is Way Too Verbose

 With a ubiquitous language, conversations among developers and expressions of the code are all derived from the same domain model.

 Eric Evans, Domain-Driven-Design

 The Problem : At the start of a project, devs and the people they're building the software for (the domain experts) are usually speaking different languages.

 I felt the same tension with my agents. Agents are usually dropped into a project and asked to figure out the jargon as they go. So they use 20 words where 1 will do.

 The Fix for this is a shared language. It's a document that helps agents decode the jargon used in the project.

Example

 Here's an example glossary (still named CONTEXT.md at that pinned commit, from before the skills renamed the convention), from my course-video-manager repo. Which one is easier to read?

- BEFORE : "There's a problem when a lesson inside a section of a course is made 'real' (i.e. given a spot in the file system)"

- AFTER : "There's a problem with the materialization cascade"

 This concision pays off session after session.

 This is built into /grill-with-docs . It's a grilling session, but that helps you build a shared language with the AI, and document hard-to-explain decisions in ADR's.

 It's hard to explain how powerful this is. It might be the single coolest technique in this repo. Try it, and see.

 Tip
 A shared language has many other benefits than reducing verbosity:

- Variables, functions and files are named consistently , using the shared language

- As a result, the codebase is easier to navigate for the agent

- The agent also spends fewer tokens on thinking , because it has access to a more concise language

 #3: The Code Doesn't Work

 "Always take small, deliberate steps. The rate of feedback is your speed limit. Never take on a task that’s too big."

 David Thomas & Andrew Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer

 The Problem : Let's say that you and the agent are aligned on what to build. What happens when the agent still produces crap?

 It's time to look at your feedback loops. Without feedback on how the code it produces actually runs, the agent will be flying blind.

 The Fix : You need the usual tranche of feedback loops: static types, browser access, and automated tests.

 For automated tests, a red-green-refactor loop is critical. This is where the agent writes a failing test first, then fixes the test. This helps give the agent a consistent level of feedback that results in far better code.

 I've built a /tdd skill you can slot into any project. It encourages red-green-refactor and gives the agent plenty of guidance on what makes good and bad tests.

 For debugging, I've also built a /diagnosing-bugs skill that wraps best debugging practices into a disciplined loop, gated phase by phase.

 #4: We Built A Ball Of Mud

 "Invest in the design of the system every day ."

 Kent Beck, Extreme Programming Explained

 "The best modules are deep. They allow a lot of functionality to be accessed through a simple interface."

 John Ousterhout, A Philosophy Of Software Design

 The Problem : Most apps built with agents are complex and hard to change. Because agents can radically speed up coding, they also accelerate software entropy. Codebases get more complex at an unprecedented rate.

 The Fix for this is a radical new approach to AI-powered development: caring about the design of the code.

 This is built in to every layer of these skills:

- /to-spec quizzes you about which modules you're touching before creating a spec

 And crucially, /improve-codebase-architecture surveys a codebase for deepening opportunities and hands you the candidates. I recommend running it on your codebase once every few days. It is a survey, not a rescue: on a genuinely old codebase it will find real candidates, but it won't untangle the mud for you.

 Summary

 Software engineering fundamentals matter more than ever. These skills are my best effort at condensing these fundamentals into repeatable practices, to help you ship the best apps of your career. Enjoy.

 Reference

 These split on one axis: who can invoke them. User-invoked skills are reachable only when you type them (e.g. /grill-me ); their job is to orchestrate. Model-invoked skills can be invoked by you or reached for automatically by the agent when the task fits; they hold the reusable discipline. A user-invoked skill may invoke model-invoked skills, but never another user-invoked one.

 Engineering

 Skills I use daily for code work.

 User-invoked

- ask-matt : Ask which skill or flow fits your situation. A router over the user-invoked skills in this repo.

- grill-with-docs : Grilling session that also builds your project's domain model, sharpening terminology and updating GLOSSARY.md and ADRs inline.

- triage : Move issues through a state machine of triage roles.

- improve-codebase-architecture : Scan a codebase for deepening opportunities, present them as a visual HTML report, then grill through whichever one you pick.

- setup-matt-pocock-skills : Configure this repo for the engineering skills (issue tracker, triage labels, domain doc layout). Run once per repo before using the other engineering skills.

- to-spec : Turn the current conversation into a spec and publish it to the issue tracker. No interview, just synthesizes what you've already discussed.

- to-tickets : Break any plan, spec, or conversation into a set of tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its blocking edges, written as text in a local file, or as native blocking links on a real tracker.

- implement : Build the work described by a spec or set of tickets, driving /tdd at pre-agreed seams and closing out with /code-review before committing.

- implement-spec : Implement a whole spec on one integration branch. Works the tickets as a task graph, running implementer subagents across the ready frontier for maximum concurrency, then closes out with /code-review .

- wayfinder : Plan a huge chunk of work, more than one agent session can hold, as a shared map of decision tickets on the issue tracker, and resolve them one at a time until the way to the destination is clear.

- retro : Suggest improvements to the coding agent's environment (navigation, automated checks, coding standards, steering files, tooling) after a session, most severe first.

 Model-invoked

- prototype : Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question, either a single shareable HTML file for state/logic questions, or several radically different UI variations toggleable from one route.

- diagnosing-bugs : Disciplined diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions: build a feedback loop that goes red on this bug → minimise → hypothesise → instrument → fix → regression-test.

- research : Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a cited Markdown file in the repo, run as a background agent.

- tdd : Test-driven development with a red-green-refactor loop. Builds features or fixes bugs one vertical slice at a time.

- domain-modeling : Actively build and sharpen a project's domain model: challenge terms against the glossary, stress-test with edge-case scenarios, and update GLOSSARY.md and ADRs inline.

- codebase-design : Shared discipline and vocabulary for designing deep modules: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface.

- code-review : Two-axis review of the diff since a fixed point: Standards (does it follow the repo's coding standards, plus a Fowler smell baseline?) and Spec (does it faithfully implement the originating issue/spec?), run as parallel sub-agents so neither pollutes the other.

- pr : The shape a pull request body should take: a summary as the smallest visual that makes the change clear, before/after evidence that it works, and a merge-danger call (one-way or two-way door, plus blast radius).

- wizard : Generate an interactive bash wizard that walks a human through steps only they can perform: provisioning infrastructure, setting up credentials or CI secrets, walking an unfamiliar third-party dashboard, or running a one-off migration or cutover.

 Productivity

 General workflow tools, not code-specific.

 User-invoked

- grill-me : Get relentlessly interviewed about a plan or design until every branch of the design tree is resolved.

- handoff : Compact the current conversation into a handoff document so...
